1→# Trace the existing EMQX chat stores

No new chat service, store, path, mode, or plugin. The implementation is already in the tree. This pass only names it.

## Transport

Every one of these chats wakes through EMQX. The production binary `op-grpc-bridge` calls `run_threetched_server`, which does `.set_doorbell(emqx_doorbell())`. That publishes `emqx.publish_wake` onto `opdbus/wake/<sha256(principal)>` with `{owner_key, seq}` only. The page re-reads private state through the plugin door. The knowledge feed uses the same wake and re-reads `ctl_plane_chatbot.list_knowledge`. The responder topic `opdbus/responder-wake/<sha256(responder)>` and the ack topic `opdbus/ack/<owner-key>` are the same broker, not extra chats.

`ChatService` (`op_chat.chat`) is mounted with `unsupported_legacy_domain`, which returns Unimplemented before a handler runs. It is not a second chat. Leave that fail-closed mount, the proto package, and the health line as they are. Do not add a listener, a guest MQTT client, or another RPC.
10→
## The stores that already exist

Private chat is the sealed `chat_response` plugin. The durable file is `CHAT_RESPONSE_DB_PATH`, default `/var/lib/op-dbus/chat-responses.db`. The private projection is the child `chat-responses` of `OP_UI_WORKSPACE_SHM_DIR`, default `/dev/shm/opdbus/ui-workspaces/chat-responses`. Pending turns are the in-memory `TurnRegistry`. The identity's persistent container Btrfs is the existing `ContainerIdentitySled.btrfs_device` (`device_path`, `mount_point`, `btrfs_uuid`). Cozo assigns that leaf; the host provisioner mounts it. Login and chat do not create a subvolume. Source does not open a second chat database on that mount, and this pass will not add one.

Project is the identity sled. `project_dispatch` reads the project catalog through `identity_sled_store()?.cozo()`. The one project database is `/var/lib/op-dbus/projects/<uuid>/cozo`, and the project container already sees that path read-only at `/project`. Do not create another project database.

UI render is already `ChatMode::UiRender`. It has an empty memory namespace and writes no memory. The session selection that names it is stored on the identity sled. The gallery contract lists `ui_render` as one of the six existing modes. There is no `ChatMode::Group` and no separate sled-feed table. Do not add a group mode or a second feed. Grouping and UI render stay categories of that existing sled selection and gallery mode list.

NotebookLM is `ChatMode::NotebookLm`, namespace `session/{session}/notebooklm/{notebook}`. The `notebooklm` plugin is the corpus owner. Its declared sinks are `semantic:qdrant` and `graph:cozo`. Episode vectorization stays `ctl_plane_chatbot.vectorize`, which delegates to `embedding_model`. Collected chat sync stays on that plugin. Do not add a NotebookLM chat service or a second vector store.
20→
## What will not change

No edits, no new path, no Cargo, no deploy. Do not move `/var/lib/op-dbus/chat-responses.db` onto the leaf, do not loosen the Lungs allowlist, and do not subscribe a guest to the responder topic.

content.text:
Considering a clean integration approach between EMQX and the execution tracker.

A clean integration path exists. The EMQX hook already validates tool-use publishes in `on_tool_use_ack`. The execution tracker already exposes `get_execution` and `verify_integrity`. The clean wire is a single shared `Arc<ExecutionTracker>`. The `TrackedToolExecutor` already writes records.

The bridge's `HookProviderService` must hold the same `Arc<ExecutionTracker>` rather than creating a new tracker. The hook should accept a tool-use ack only when `tracker.get_execution(&ack.turn_id)` returns a record whose hash matches `ack.turn_hash` and integrity holds. A miss or mismatch still fails closed. No new hooks, topics, protos, or second tracker are needed. The broker continues to see only ack IDs. The tracker is an in-memory ring limited by `max_history`.

The tracker is not durable. A process restart or eviction can cause `get_execution` to return None, so the hook may reject a valid ack. This is fail-closed and acceptable.

The bridge currently builds its own private tracker inside `ChatActor`. The integration requires passing that same `Arc` into `HookProviderService::new` or `with_queue`.

The actor and hook may not run in the same process. ChatActor is constructed in op-chat, not the bridge server. The tracker is created wherever ChatActor or TrackedToolExecutor lives. If those live outside the bridge, sharing an Arc across processes is impossible.

The bridge depends on op-chat, which re-exports TrackedToolExecutor and op-execution-tracker.

op-chat likely does not re-export ExecutionTracker. The bridge may need a direct dependency on op-execution-tracker.

HookProviderService can reuse the existing Arc<ExecutionTracker> directly. It would compare the execution hash against the turn hash inside on_tool_use_ack. This avoids a new file, hook name, or chat_response change. The tracker must remain in-memory and is not constructed by the bridge process.

The bridge should own the ExecutionTracker. ChatActor must receive that Arc instead of constructing its own tracker. This gives one tracker to two callers.

# Point the existing EMQX ack hook at the existing execution tracker

Yes. One lookup, no new hook and no new tracker.

## The join

`HookProviderService::on_tool_use_ack` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/emqx_hook_provider.rs` is already the publish decision for `opdbus/ack/<owner-key>`. It parses `owner_key`, `turn_id`, and `turn_hash`, then calls `verify_tool_use_ack`, which asks `chat_turn_receipt_exists`. That Cozo probe is the old `chat_response` path. Stop using it.

`crates/op-execution-tracker` already stores the tool run. `ExecutionTracker::get_execution(id)` returns the record, and `ExecutionRecord::hash` is `exec_hash`. `TrackedToolExecutor` is the writer. `op-grpc-bridge` already depends on `op-chat`, which owns that executor.

Give `HookProviderService` the same `Arc<ExecutionTracker>` the executor writes. Do not call `ExecutionTracker::new` in the hook. `ChatActor` currently builds a private tracker; that constructor should take the bridge's Arc instead, so there is still one tracker.

On an ack, `get_execution(&ack.turn_id)` must return a record whose `hash()` equals `ack.turn_hash` and whose `verify_integrity()` is true. Anything else stays the current fail-closed deny (`stop_with(false)` and the flagged broker event). The broker still receives no tool body.

## What stays

`emqx.rs` keeps `REGISTERED_HOOKS` and `list_hooks` / `get_hook_status` / `configure_hooks`. The loopback mTLS `HookProvider` mount stays the only ExHook server. Do not add a hook name, a topic, a proto, or a second tracker (`op-core`'s copy stays unused). Do not move private, project, group, UI render, or NotebookLM storage.

The tracker is an in-memory ring. After eviction or restart, `get_execution` returns nothing and the ack is refused. That matches fail-closed. This change does not make the ring durable and does not put the receipt back on `chat_response`.

# Trace the existing EMQX hooks

`chat_response` is old. Do not extend it, and do not add a second hook, a second tracker, or a second chat service. This pass only names the two hook files that are already in the tree and where they stop.

## The two hook files

`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/emqx.rs` is the broker plugin. It owns `REGISTERED_HOOKS` (the twenty `client.*`, `session.*`, and `message.*` names), and the methods `list_hooks`, `get_hook_status`, and `configure_hooks`. `configure_hooks` accepts only that exact set, aimed at the loopback mTLS ExHook server named `opdbus`.

`crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/emqx_hook_provider.rs` is the other file: `HookProviderService`, the `emqx.exhook.v3.HookProvider` that EMQX calls. `run_threetched_server` mounts that one service on the loopback mTLS listener. `on_message_publish` records a digested broker event through `MutationEngine` and, for a matching persona trigger, enqueues the existing agent run. An `opdbus/ack/<owner-key>` publish goes to `on_tool_use_ack`.

## Where that ack still points

`on_tool_use_ack` calls `wake_doorbell::verify_tool_use_ack`, which calls `CozoGraphShuttle::chat_turn_receipt_exists`. That is the old `chat_response` receipt. The hook does not call `op_execution_tracker::ExecutionTracker`.

The execution tracker that already exists is `crates/op-execution-tracker`. `op-chat`'s `TrackedToolExecutor` records tool runs there. `op-workflows` and `op-dynamic-loader` each construct their own tracker. `op-core` has a separate `ExecutionTracker`; `forced_execution.rs` leaves that import commented out. The bridge never holds either tracker, so the mounted hook cannot see those records.

## What this pass will not do

No new `hooks.rs`, no second `HookProvider`, no second `ExecutionTracker`, no change to `REGISTERED_HOOKS`, no revival of `chat_response`, no Cargo, and no deploy. Private chat stays on the identity's existing container Btrfs leaf (`ContainerIdentitySled.btrfs_device`). Project stays on the identity sled. Group and UI render stay categories of that sled selection. NotebookLM stays the existing plugin, which vectorizes its own collected chat. All of those wakes stay on the one EMQX broker.

The subscription currently writes raw execution content including output_summary, which may contain PII. The original schema filters out PII fields such as goal_text, reasoning_summary, and decision_output before vectorization.

The filter should drop fields marked private by the original schema, including output_summary. It should follow plan_vectorization exactly when pii_flagged is true.

"Filter the subscription" means restricting which events enter the vectorization pipeline, not merely stripping fields from payloads. The original schema defines this boundary via its x-opdbus-private attributes.

content.text:
A function will filter execution records through the sealed method schema using described_fields. Only that filtered text will be stored in sled.

Tools missing from the schema will be skipped entirely. The tool name is split on the first dot to separate plugin and method identifiers.

The filter applies only to the method's arguments schema. Raw output summaries are excluded unless explicitly described in the schema. Only fields described by the schema will be embedded.

Execution IDs and hashes will be kept out of the vectorization text. Only the schema-described argument lines will form the content string stored in sled.

The stored content will be formatted as `tool: plugin.method`, `subid: ...`, and `field (description): value`. If no fields are described, only the tool name and subscription ID will be recorded. A missing plugin schema causes the event to be dropped entirely.

The filter will be applied inside `write_execution_on_sled` before content is assembled. It calls `schema_filtered_execution`, and if that returns `None` the function returns early and skips the sled write entirely.

The sealed plugin schema is already the filter that runs before vectorization: it keeps only described fields and drops private ones. The sled subscription will use that filter before it writes an execution.

content.text:
1→---
name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  TypeSafe integration craft for System One models (sometimes called Decision Models) such as Jev,
  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.
---

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→
## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".

  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.

  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".

  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context

  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.

  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and

  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".

  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our

  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.

  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:

- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks

Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

that fits the problem you're solving.

1→# JEV schema judgments
When JEV may rename tched to threetched, and 2026-10-26 crate-scan counts and scope.

## Preference

- Use JEV (TypeSafe) to judge fixes that replace leftover tched-bridge references with the captured threetched schema.
- Do not blindly rename leftover tched_router identifiers in op-grpc-bridge to threetched. tched names can be instance locators or legacy transport. Only stale hand-rolled schema references should be rewired to the pinned capture.
- Fix a judged tched defect literally line by line, not as a blind rename, and without search tools.
- If a match containing tched is not the defect, consult JEV for context and for where the code lives in zeroclaw when it is not the hand-rolled implementation.
10→- Reviewed tched hits are marked by renaming them to threetched only after JEV classifies the token. Unjudged spellings stay so addressed items stay visible.
- JEV choices are exactly removed_hand_rolled_bridge, pinned_threetched_schema, zeroclaw_0_8_4_command, our_grpc_envelope, and unrelated.
- Inline-edit an identifier to threetched only when removed_hand_rolled_bridge confidence is at least 0.7.
- Reject a rename when zeroclaw_0_8_4_command is at least 0.7. Abstain when confidence is between 0.3 and 0.7.
- Real ZeroClaw 0.8.4 CLI command strings, including skills, models, providers, and plugin, stay unchanged. Do not rename environment-variable keys, D-Bus object paths, or on-disk socket paths.
- Do not ask JEV whether to rename.
- When JEV judges a tched token is the removed hand-rolled bridge or an own schema/gRPC label, edit the source in the same step.
- A receipt only logs edits that already landed. Do not stop at a receipt or invent edits when no judged defect exists.
- During the scan do not run cargo, tests, clippy, fmt, or deploy, and do not use ripgrep to hunt tched tokens.
- Per-crate reads use receipt /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/<crate>/receipt.md under /srv/git/odbus-verified.
20→- A crate agent must not edit other crates, HANDOFF.md, SIGNALS.md, or vendor/.
- op-uds-relay is excluded from the workspace and op-ml is disabled, so neither is in the scan.
- On 2026-10-26 the user first narrowed the threetched review to the bridge and cache crates only, then later the same day asked JEV ("jefe") about every endpoint, method, and route referenced by tched/threetched naming, across all crates rather than only the bridge or cache.
- Inline changes should wait on a per-item JEV judgment.
- Real zeroclaw command names should not be renamed just because they appear near tched/threetched references.
- Owner-fixed threetched-fs names must not be renamed: Cargo package tched-fs, plugin tched_fs, directory crates/threetched-fs, mount /run/mounts/3tchedFS.
- Open vSwitch bridge names are not the removed tched-bridge.
- 2026-10-26 line-by-line scan of op-dbus-model (390 lines: Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, src/models.rs, SPEC.md, compare-op-dbus-model.md) found no tched identifiers, including tched_router, tched-bridge, Tched, TCHED, 3tched, and threetched. JEV was not called and nothing was renamed. Receipt: /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/op-dbus-model/receipt.md.
- 2026-10-26 scan of op-compliance (Cargo.toml 12 lines, src/lib.rs 324 lines) found no tched identifiers. JEV was not called and nothing was renamed. Scan complete. Receipt: /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/op-compliance/receipt.md.
- Full line-by-line read of /srv/git/odbus-verified/crates/op-cache found no tched, tched_router, tched-bridge, Tched, TCHED, or 3tched tokens, so JEV was not called and no source edit was made. Receipt: /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/op-cache/receipt.md.
30→- Absence of that string is not a pass if hand-rolled plugin, router, or bridge schema-cache code remains.
- Btrfs, workflow, and NUMA caches must not be renamed to threetched.
- Literal "threetched" in crates rs/proto/toml is concentrated in op-plugins (17), op-grpc-bridge (17), and threetched-fs (15), plus op-chat (3), op-chat-responder (2), and one file each in op-web, op-state-store, op-snowball, op-llm, op-deployment, op-cozo-store, op-cognitive, and op-blob.
- A broader token search for tched in rs/proto also hits op-cozo-store (9), op-network (4), op-mcp, op-state, op-mcp-aggregator, op-identity, op-execution-tracker, and op-agents among others. No line audit of those counts was finished.
- On 2026-10-26 the threetched-jev-per-crate review covers every crate that references the threetched side: skills, plugins, models, providers, and each endpoint, method, and route. JEV judges each reference; inline edits only after that judgment; no Cargo or deploy.
- One-crate agents cover op-plugins, threetched-fs, op-llm, op-chat, op-web, op-cognitive, op-mcp, op-network, op-cozo-store, op-agents, op-chat-responder, op-state-store, op-blob, op-deployment, op-snowball, op-identity, op-execution-tracker, op-mcp-aggregator, and op-state. op-grpc-bridge and op-cache agents stay in place.
- Receipts go to /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/<crate>/receipt.md, one row per reference.

# Primitives (Questions)

> The TypeSafe question types, the typed answers they return, how to choose between them, and how to ask several at once.

TypeSafe's primitives are the small, typed building blocks you compose in code. They come in pairs: a question defines one judgment for a [System One model](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md) to make about a [state](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), and its answer is the typed value that comes back. You compose the answers in your code to make decisions. Each question type returns a different shape of answer.

| Type | What it answers | Returns |
| - | - | - |
| [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Which of these options? | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Which level? | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Is this true? | `noul` (0 to 1) |

You can ask one question or send several together. Every question in a request sees the same state, is evaluated independently, and returns a typed answer under the ID you chose.

## Ask for one snap judgment per question

System One models are built for fast, focused judgments. Ask for a judgment a knowledgeable person makes in a second given the right context. "Does this message convey urgency?" is a good question. "Analyze this message and determine the best course of action" is not. That needs slow reasoning, and it is a signal to break the task into small questions and compose the answers in code.

If the judgment you want depends on several independent factors, ask about each factor separately and combine the answers with your own logic. Instead of "rate this startup pitch", ask about market size, technical feasibility, and differentiation, then weight them in code based on their relative importance. When priorities shift, change the value of weights rather than rewriting a prompt. [Ask multiple questions together](#ask-***) shows how to do this.

## Define a question

Every question has an ID, a `type`, and `instructions`. Choice and Score questions also take `criteria`, which define the options for a Choice question or the levels for a Score. Noul questions accept `criteria` as an optional clarification of what yes and no mean.

* ID. The key you pick, such as `refund_requested`. It identifies the answer in the response.
* `type`. One of `choice`, `score`, or `noul`.
* `instructions`. The question you are asking about the state. This is where your evaluation logic goes. Write it as a clear, specific question, or as a statement for the model to judge. A string is enough for most questions. It can also be an object or an array, which puts the question in one field and the data it refers to in others; see [Use structure in the questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md#use-structure-in-the-questions).
* `criteria`. The possible answers: a map of options for a Choice question, an ordered list of levels for a Score, and an optional description of yes and no for a Noul. Each question type's page covers its shape.

This question asks whether a customer requested a refund:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul

questions = {
    "refund_requested": Noul(
        instructions="Does the customer request a refund?",
    ),
}
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Question IDs are for your code. They are not sent to the model. Write the complete question in `instructions`, even when the ID seems self-explanatory.

## Choose a question type

Pick the type that matches the shape of the answer you need.

* **Choice** fits when the answer is one of a known set of options with no order between them: routing a ticket to a department, classifying a document type, detecting a programming language. Give the full list of options, and add an `other` or `none of the above` option when the list might not cover every input.

* **Score** fits when the answer falls on a spectrum and you can describe what each point on that spectrum means: bug severity, customer frustration, skill level. The levels are yours to define, and the model returns a position along them.

* **Noul** fits a clean yes/no question where the probability itself is the useful signal: does this message contain personally identifiable information, is the customer requesting a refund, does the resume mention distributed systems.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Use Noul for a yes/no judgment and Score to measure a position on a spectrum. "Is this candidate strong in Python?" needs a clear definition of "strong". A Noul value of 0.5 means the model gives yes and no equal probability. It does not mean the candidate has a medium skill level. An unclear definition makes that probability hard to interpret.
>
> If you want to measure skill level, use a Score with defined levels, such as no experience, some familiarity, daily use, and deep expertise. If you need a yes/no decision, define the condition clearly, such as "Does the resume state that the candidate has used Python at work?"

If two types both seem to fit, prefer the one whose answer your code can act on directly. A Choice between `refund`, `rebook`, and `information` maps straight onto three code paths. A Score of customer frustration maps onto a threshold. A Noul maps onto an `if`.

## What comes back

Answers are primitives too. Each question type returns a typed value that your code can compare, threshold, sort, pass into further logic, or put into the state of a follow-up request (see [When one question depends on another](#when-one-question-depends-on-another)).

| Type | Answer fields | How to read it |
| - | - | - |
| Choice | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` | `choice` is the selected option. `probabilities` is the distribution across every option. `confidence` summarizes how peaked that distribution is. |
| Score | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence` | `score` is a position along your levels, and can fall between two of them. `legend` repeats the levels by number. `probabilities` is the distribution across levels. |
| Noul | `noul` | The probability that the answer is yes. Near 1 is a strong yes, near 0 a strong no, near 0.5 uncertain. Noul has no separate `confidence`. |

Two properties of these answers make them composable:

* **Every answer is constrained to the options you supplied.** The model returns a probability distribution over your options or levels, never a value outside them. Your code never has to recover a value from generated prose.
* **Every answer is independent.** One question's answer is not hidden context for another. You can add or remove questions without changing the others' results.

Some question types also return `confidence`; each type's page says whether its answers include it. [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) explains how to use it to decide when to act automatically and when to escalate to a person.

## Reference specific fields

The content being evaluated, the [state](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), is often a JSON object with several parts: a conversation, a record, a policy. When a question is about one of those parts, name it in the `instructions` with a dot-and-index path to its key, including the backticks. The model then knows which part of the state to judge.

Take the support conversation from the State page:

```json theme={null}
{
  "ticket": {
    "subject": "Duplicate charge",
    "messages": [
      {"from": "customer", "text": "I was charged twice for order A-104. Please refund the duplicate."},
      {"from": "support", "text": "We are checking the charges."}
    ]
  },
  "order": {
    "id": "A-104",
    "charges": [
      {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"},
      {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"}
    ]
  },
  "refund_policy": "Duplicate charges are eligible for a refund."
}
```

These two questions point at the customer's message, the policy, and the charges by path:

```python theme={null}
questions = {
    "refund_requested": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Does `ticket.messages[0].text` request a refund?",
    },
    "policy_supports_refund": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": (
            "Does `refund_policy` support the refund requested "
            "in `ticket.messages[0].text`, given `order.charges`?"
        ),
    },
}
```

Explicit paths make it clear which parts of a structured state should inform each judgment. See [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md) for how to structure the input.

## Ask multiple questions together

Send every question that uses the same state in one request. You can mix question types freely. System One models evaluate every question in a request in parallel. Adding questions barely changes the response time and costs only the tokens for the extra questions, which are cheap. Asking a question you might not need is close to free.

This request classifies a customer message, checks for urgency, and scores frustration all at once:

Try it in the Playground →

Our [client SDKs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk.md) provide typed questions and answers. In Python, pass a `questions` dictionary of `Choice`, `Noul`, and `Score` objects to `client.system_one(...)`. This request sends a ticket and a refund policy once and gets a typed answer for each question:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient

state = {
    "ticket_message": "My flight was cancelled. Can I get a refund?",
    "refund_policy": "Cancelled flights are eligible for a full refund.",
}

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    response = client.system_one(
        state=state,
        questions={
            "refund_requested": Noul(
                instructions="Does `ticket_message` request a refund?",
            ),
            "request_type": Choice(
                instructions="What is the main request in `ticket_message`?",
                criteria={
                    "refund": "The customer wants money returned.",
                    "rebooking": "The customer wants a replacement flight.",
                    "information": "The customer is asking for information only.",
                },
            ),
            "frustration": Score(
                instructions="How frustrated does the customer appear in `ticket_message`?",
                criteria=[
                    "Calm and neutral.",
                    "Concerned but civil.",
                    "Very angry or using strong language.",
                ],
            ),
        },
    )

print(response.answers["refund_requested"].noul)
print(response.answers["request_type"].choice)
print(response.answers["frustration"].score)
```

See [client SDKs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk.md) for installation and usage in your language.

### Ask speculative questions

Ask every question your code might need, including ones whose answer only matters for some inputs, and let the code decide which answers to use. If a ticket turns out not to be a bug report, ignore the severity answer. We call this the [Speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md) pattern. The [Parallel questions cookbook](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md) shows how batching 13 questions into one call is 11.5x cheaper and 9.6x faster than 13 separate calls, with no change in the answers.

> [!TIP]
>
> Coding agents fall into the one question per call habit more than people do. The [TypeSafe agent skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill.md#installation) tells your agent to put many questions in each call, including ones that only matter for some inputs.

### How many questions you can ask

There is no limit on the number of questions in a request. What limits a request is its size: it has to fit the model's [per-request context and per-question context](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md#context-length).

Questions are often short compared with the `state`, in which case the `state` takes up most of both. If your questions don't all fit in one request, one option is to spread them across several requests with the same `state`.

### Split a complex judgment into several questions

A judgment that depends on several things is best split into one question per thing. Combine the answers in your code, giving each a weight for its relative importance. The weights are yours. When the combined result doesn't match what your team would decide, change them in code and run again. Adding questions barely changes the response time because they run in parallel within one request. The split costs a few extra question tokens.

For example, ticket priority might be built from three Score questions: how severe the bug is, how frustrated the customer is, and how much the report gives an engineer to work with. The Score page walks through this request and the code that normalizes and weights the answers in [Splitting a complex judgment into several Scores](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md#splitting-a-complex-judgment-into-several-score-questions). This technique is called the [Composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) pattern.

### When one question depends on another

Questions in the same request are independent: one answer does not become context for another question. If a later judgment depends on an earlier answer, make a second request in code. The dependency is real only when your code cannot build the second request until it has the first answer: it needs the answer to fetch more data for the state, to decide what the state is made of, or to pick the next question's options. Otherwise, ask the questions together and combine their answers in code.

Two requests are the exception, not the rule. If the second request's questions could have been asked against the original state, ask them in the first request and let the code ignore the ones it doesn't need. Three cookbooks make a second request for a real reason. [Skill suggestion](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md) ranks 182 skills in one request, then fetches the full text of the top three and judges them again against that better evidence. [Structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md) asks whether each line break split a sentence, merges lines into blocks from those answers, then classifies the blocks, which did not exist until the first request had answered. [Hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md) uses each Choice answer to decide which options the next request offers.

See [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) for guidance on breaking a workflow into focused judgments.

## Next steps

> **[Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md)**
>
> Pick one option from a fixed list.

> **[Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md)**
>
> Rate the state along ordered levels.

> **[Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md)**
>
> Get the probability that a statement is true.

To see how these compose into system architectures, head to [Patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns.md).

* **Score** fits when the answer falls on a spectrum and you can describe what each point on that spectrum means: bug severity, customer frustration, skill level. The levels are yours to define, and the model returns a position along them.

* **Noul** fits a clean yes/no question where the probability itself is the useful signal: does this message contain personally identifiable information, is the customer requesting a refund, does the resume mention distributed systems.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Use Noul for a yes/no judgment and Score to measure a position on a spectrum. "Is this candidate strong in Python?" needs a clear definition of "strong". A Noul value of 0.5 means the model gives yes and no equal probability. It does not mean the candidate has a medium skill level. An unclear definition makes that probability hard to interpret.
>
> If you want to measure skill level, use a Score with defined levels, such as no experience, some familiarity, daily use, and deep expertise. If you need a yes/no decision, define the condition clearly, such as "Does the resume state that the candidate has used Python at work?"

If two types both seem to fit, prefer the one whose answer your code can act on directly. A Choice between `refund`, `rebook`, and `information` maps straight onto three code paths. A Score of customer frustration maps onto a threshold. A Noul maps onto an `if`.

## What comes back

Answers are primitives too. Each question type returns a typed value that your code can compare, threshold, sort, pass into further logic, or put into the state of a follow-up request (see [When one question depends on another](#when-one-question-depends-on-another)).

| Type | Answer fields | How to read it |
| - | - | - |
| Choice | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` | `choice` is the selected option. `probabilities` is the distribution across every option. `confidence` summarizes how peaked that distribution is. |
| Score | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence` | `score` is a position along your levels, and can fall between two of them. `legend` repeats the levels by number. `probabilities` is the distribution across levels. |
| Noul | `noul` | The probability that the answer is yes. Near 1 is a strong yes, near 0 a strong no, near 0.5 uncertain. Noul has no separate `confidence`. |

Two properties of these answers make them composable:

* **Every answer is constrained to the options you supplied.** The model returns a probability distribution over your options or levels, never a value outside them. Your code never has to recover a value from generated prose.
* **Every answer is independent.** One question's answer is not hidden context for another. You can add or remove questions without changing the others' results.

Some question types also return `confidence`; each type's page says whether its answers include it. [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) explains how to use it to decide when to act automatically and when to escalate to a person.

## Reference specific fields

The content being evaluated, the [state](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), is often a JSON object with several parts: a conversation, a record, a policy. When a question is about one of those parts, name it in the `instructions` with a dot-and-index path to its key, including the backticks. The model then knows which part of the state to judge.

Take the support conversation from the State page:

```json theme={null}
{
  "ticket": {
    "subject": "Duplicate charge",
    "messages": [
      {"from": "customer", "text": "I was charged twice for order A-104. Please refund the duplicate."},
      {"from": "support", "text": "We are checking the charges."}
    ]
  },
  "order": {
    "id": "A-104",
    "charges": [
      {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"},
      {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"}
    ]
  },
  "refund_policy": "Duplicate charges are eligible for a refund."
}
```

These two questions point at the customer's message, the policy, and the charges by path:

```python theme={null}
questions = {
    "refund_requested": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Does `ticket.messages[0].text` request a refund?",
    },
    "policy_supports_refund": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": (
            "Does `refund_policy` support the refund requested "
            "in `ticket.messages[0].text`, given `order.charges`?"
        ),
    },
}
```

Explicit paths make it clear which parts of a structured state should inform each judgment. See [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md) for how to structure the input.

## Ask multiple questions together

Send every question that uses the same state in one request. You can mix question types freely. System One models evaluate every question in a request in parallel. Adding questions barely changes the response time and costs only the tokens for the extra questions, which are cheap. Asking a question you might not need is close to free.

This request classifies a customer message, checks for urgency, and scores frustration all at once:

Try it in the Playground →

Our [client SDKs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk.md) provide typed questions and answers. In Python, pass a `questions` dictionary of `Choice`, `Noul`, and `Score` objects to `client.system_one(...)`. This request sends a ticket and a refund policy once and gets a typed answer for each question:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient

state = {
    "ticket_message": "My flight was cancelled. Can I get a refund?",
    "refund_policy": "Cancelled flights are eligible for a full refund.",
}

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    response = client.system_one(
        state=state,
        questions={
            "refund_requested": Noul(
                instructions="Does `ticket_message` request a refund?",
            ),
            "request_type": Choice(
                instructions="What is the main request in `ticket_message`?",
                criteria={
                    "refund": "The customer wants money returned.",
                    "rebooking": "The customer wants a replacement flight.",
                    "information": "The customer is asking for information only.",
                },
            ),
            "frustration": Score(
                instructions="How frustrated does the customer appear in `ticket_message`?",
                criteria=[
                    "Calm and neutral.",
                    "Concerned but civil.",
                    "Very angry or using strong language.",
                ],
            ),
        },
    )

print(response.answers["refund_requested"].noul)
print(response.answers["request_type"].choice)
print(response.answers["frustration"].score)
```

See [client SDKs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk.md) for installation and usage in your language.

### Ask speculative questions

Ask every question your code might need, including ones whose answer only matters for some inputs, and let the code decide which answers to use. If a ticket turns out not to be a bug report, ignore the severity answer. We call this the [Speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md) pattern. The [Parallel questions cookbook](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md) shows how batching 13 questions into one call is 11.5x cheaper and 9.6x faster than 13 separate calls, with no change in the answers.

> [!TIP]
>
> Coding agents fall into the one question per call habit more than people do. The [TypeSafe agent skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill.md#installation) tells your agent to put many questions in each call, including ones that only matter for some inputs.

### How many questions you can ask

There is no limit on the number of questions in a request. What limits a request is its size: it has to fit the model's [per-request context and per-question context](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md#context-length).

Questions are often short compared with the `state`, in which case the `state` takes up most of both. If your questions don't all fit in one request, one option is to spread them across several requests with the same `state`.

### Split a complex judgment into several questions

A judgment that depends on several things is best split into one question per thing. Combine the answers in your code, giving each a weight for its relative importance. The weights are yours. When the combined result doesn't match what your team would decide, change them in code and run again. Adding questions barely changes the response time because they run in parallel within one request. The split costs a few extra question tokens.

For example, ticket priority might be built from three Score questions: how severe the bug is, how frustrated the customer is, and how much the report gives an engineer to work with. The Score page walks through this request and the code that normalizes and weights the answers in [Splitting a complex judgment into several Scores](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md#splitting-a-complex-judgment-into-several-score-questions). This technique is called the [Composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) pattern.

### When one question depends on another

Questions in the same request are independent: one answer does not become context for another question. If a later judgment depends on an earlier answer, make a second request in code. The dependency is real only when your code cannot build the second request until it has the first answer: it needs the answer to fetch more data for the state, to decide what the state is made of, or to pick the next question's options. Otherwise, ask the questions together and combine their answers in code.

Two requests are the exception, not the rule. If the second request's questions could have been asked against the original state, ask them in the first request and let the code ignore the ones it doesn't need. Three cookbooks make a second request for a real reason. [Skill suggestion](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md) ranks 182 skills in one request, then fetches the full text of the top three and judges them again against that better evidence. [Structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md) asks whether each line break split a sentence, merges lines into blocks from those answers, then classifies the blocks, which did not exist until the first request had answered. [Hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md) uses each Choice answer to decide which options the next request offers.

See [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) for guidance on breaking a workflow into focused judgments.

## Next steps

> **[Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md)**
>
> Pick one option from a fixed list.

> **[Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md)**
>
> Rate the state along ordered levels.

> **[Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md)**
>
> Get the probability that a statement is true.

To see how these compose into system architectures, head to [Patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns.md).

I'll use object-style criteria with what and not_for fields to match the working requests. I'll fall back to strings if the API rejects them. Now fetching the noul documentation.

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Noul

> A Noul question asks the TypeSafe model to evaluate a yes/no question and return the probability that the answer is yes.

Use a Noul when the answer is yes or no. For example, does this message ask for a refund, does this resume mention distributed systems, does this comment contain personal data. If the answer is one of several options, use a [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md). If it's a position on a spectrum, use a [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md). [Choose a question type](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives#choose-a-question-type) compares all three.

A Noul answer is a single number representing the probability that the answer is yes where 0 means no and 1 means yes.

## Request structure

The POST request body to the [TypeSafe API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api) has the same three top-level fields as any other question type: `state`, which is the content to evaluate; `model`; and `questions`. Each Noul question has the following fields:

* `type`: Always `"noul"`.
* `instructions`: The yes/no question the model answers, or a statement for it to judge.
* `criteria`: Optional. An object with `true` and `false` descriptions of what a yes and a no mean.

Below is a request where the state is a support message and the two questions are whether the customer wants a person and whether they have contacted support before:

Try it in the Playground →

You choose the question ids, `is_human_escalation` and `is_repeat_contact` here. The ids are not sent to the model. Each answer is returned under the same id. The first question relies on `instructions` alone. The second adds `criteria` to say what counts as a yes and what counts as a no.

With the [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), the same questions are `Noul` objects:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, NoulCriteria, TypeSafeClient

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    response = client.system_one(
        model="jev-latest",
        state="I have asked three times now. Can I please just talk to a real person?",
        questions={
            "is_human_escalation": Noul(
                instructions="Is the customer asking for a human agent?",
            ),
            "is_repeat_contact": Noul(
                instructions="Has the customer contacted support about this before?",
                criteria=NoulCriteria(
                    true="Mentions a prior attempt, ticket, or that they have asked before",
                    false="No sign of any previous contact",
                ),
            ),
        },
    )

    print(response.answers["is_human_escalation"].noul)
    print(response.answers["is_repeat_contact"].noul)
```

The `system_one` method and the `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` endpoint are both named after [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), TypeSafe's AI model. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) covers where to use it in your code.

If you're using a coding agent, install the [TypeSafe agent skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill.md#installation) first so it knows the request and response shapes.

> [!NOTE]
>
> `instructions` can be a string, an object, or an array. Start with a string. Use an object when the question needs data alongside it, such as a record to compare the state against, or when part of the question is built by your code. [Use structure in the questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md#use-structure-in-the-questions) explains when structure helps, and [the example below](#structured-instructions) shows it with questions built in code.

## Response structure

The response has one entry in `answers` per question, under the ids from the request:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.13.0",
  "answers": {
    "is_human_escalation": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.99
    },
    "is_repeat_contact": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.93
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 360,
    "output_tokens": 39
  }
}
```

Both answers here are close to 1. The customer says "talk to a real person", so `is_human_escalation` is 0.99. "I have asked three times now" matches the `true` description of `is_repeat_contact`, so it is 0.93.

## Reading a Noul

The number is the answer and the certainty in one. A value near 1 is a strong yes. A value near 0 is a strong no. A value near 0.5 means the model gives yes and no similar probability.

The table below shows recorded `jev-1.13.0` answers to the `is_human_escalation` question for different customer messages:

| State | `noul` |
| - | - |
| Thanks, that fixed it! | 0.02 |
| How do I reset my password? | 0.07 |
| I need this sorted today, whatever it takes. | 0.26 |
| Are you a bot? | 0.40 |
| Is there any way to speak to someone about my invoice? | 0.84 |
| I have asked three times now. Can I please just talk to a real person? | 0.99 |

The first two and the last two are clear. "I need this sorted today" is urgent but never asks for a person, and gets 0.26. "Are you a bot?" hints at wanting a human without asking for one, and the model splits almost evenly at 0.40. Both are the kind of message where a decision needs to be made based on a threshold in your code.

There is no separate `confidence` value for a Noul, unlike a [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) or a [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md). A Noul's probability distribution has only two outcomes, yes and no, so the single `noul` value describes it completely. A Choice or Score spreads probability over several options or levels, and `confidence` summarizes that spread.

Most often your code thresholds `noul` into a boolean:

```python theme={null}
wants_human = response.answers["is_human_escalation"].noul > 0.9

if wants_human:
    route_to_agent(ticket)
else:
    route_to_bot(ticket)
```

A good starting point is 0.7 for yes and 0.3 for no. Often you only care whether the answer is yes, and 0.7 is the only threshold you need. Where to set it depends on the cost of being wrong. Raise it when acting on a false yes is expensive, such as paging someone or issuing a refund. Lower it when missing a true yes is expensive, such as failing to flag a safety issue. Avoid fitting thresholds closely to a handful of test cases. Values between 0.3 and 0.7 can go to a person rather than either code path. That is the same three-way split the [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md#three-paths-for-using-confidence-in-your-code) page describes for Choice and Score answers.

A Noul value runs from 0 to 1, but it's not a scale of the thing you asked about. It is the probability that the answer is yes. If the question is really about degree, the value does not measure the degree. Below, "Is the candidate strong in Python?" is asked about four candidates, next to a [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) with four levels: no experience, some familiarity, regular use in a job, deep expertise.

| Candidate | Noul: "Is the candidate strong in Python?" | Score: "How much Python experience does the candidate have?" |
| - | - | - |
| My experience is in Java and Go. I have not used Python. | 0.03 | 0.0 (No experience) |
| I have used Python occasionally for small scripts alongside my main Java work. | 0.14 | 1.0 (Some familiarity) |
| I used Python every day for two years in my last job, mostly data pipelines. | 0.81 | 2.05 (Regular use in a job) |
| I have written Python daily for eight years, including maintaining a large Django codebase. | 0.92 | 2.89 (Deep expertise) |

The Noul judges one proposition, "strong", and the values are how likely it is. You could create levels in the 0 to 1 range in your code, such as 0.3 to 0.7 for "some experience", but the model will not see them, so nothing in the answer was judged against them. A middle value can mean medium experience or an unclear case, and the spacing between candidates is not something you chose. The Score judges each level description on its own, so every candidate landed on or near a level you wrote, and the returned probabilities show how the model divided its judgment between levels. If you disagree, reword a level and run it again. [Choose a question type](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives#choose-a-question-type) explains the distinction.

## Writing a Noul question

Ask one yes/no question per Noul. If a question has two conditions, such as "Is the customer angry and asking for a refund?", the model has to judge both at once and the value means less. Ask two Nouls and combine them in code.

Phrase the question so that a high value means yes. "Does the message contain personal data?" is clear. "Is the message free of personal data?" inverts the meaning, and code that reads it later will get it backwards.

A statement works as well as a question. For "The customer is requesting a refund", a value near 1 means the statement is true. Try both phrasings with your own data to see which works better.

Make the boundary between yes and no unambiguous. "Does this candidate have any Python experience?" works well because "any" leaves no middle ground. When the boundary is subtle, add `criteria` with `true` and `false` descriptions, as the `is_repeat_contact` question above does. The instruction is enough for most Nouls, so try your questions with and without `criteria` and keep whichever gives better answers on your documents.

## Good practice: ask more than one question per call

For a checklist of conditions, ask many Noul questions in one request: one question per condition, and the code decides what the combination means. Questions are evaluated in parallel, so adding Nouls barely changes the response time. [Ask multiple questions together](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives#ask-***) explains this in more detail.

## Handling multiple Noul answers in code

The two-question request above gives the code enough to route the message. The example below escalates to a person when the customer asks for one, and raises the priority when they have been in touch before. A value in the middle on either question goes to a reviewer instead of a code path:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, NoulCriteria, TypeSafeClient

SUPPORT_QUESTIONS = {
    "is_human_escalation": Noul(
        instructions="Is the customer asking for a human agent?",
    ),
    "is_repeat_contact": Noul(
        instructions="Has the customer contacted support about this before?",
        criteria=NoulCriteria(
            true="Mentions a prior attempt, ticket, or that they have asked before",
            false="No sign of any previous contact",
        ),
    ),
}

YES = 0.7
NO = 0.3


def route(message: str) -> None:
    with TypeSafeClient() as client:
        response = client.system_one(
            model="jev-latest",
            state=message,
            questions=SUPPORT_QUESTIONS,
        )
    answers = response.answers

    wants_human = answers["is_human_escalation"].noul
    repeat = answers["is_repeat_contact"].noul

    if NO < wants_human < YES or NO < repeat < YES:
        # The model isn't sure either way. Let a person decide.
        send_to_review(message)
        return

    priority = "high" if repeat >= YES else "normal"
    if wants_human >= YES:
        route_to_agent(message, priority=priority)
    else:
        route_to_bot(message, priority=priority)
```

For the message above, the noul answer value for `is_human_escalation` is 0.99 and `is_repeat_contact` is 0.93, so the code routes it to an agent at high priority. The message "How do I reset my password?" is 0.07 on both questions and is routed to the bot.

The thresholds live in your code. If reviewers see too many messages, narrow the gap between `NO` and `YES`. If too many wrong routes get through, widen it. If you later need to know whether the message mentions a payment, or whether it contains personal data, add another Noul to `SUPPORT_QUESTIONS`. The request count stays at one.

## Structured instructions

Instructions can be an object instead of a string, with the question in one field and supplementary data in the others. [Use structure in the questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md#use-structure-in-the-questions) covers when that helps. Here it's used for a question built using code: a resume that has just arrived is compared against records in a candidate database that might be the same person. Each record goes into a `potential_duplicate` field as it is, the `question` is the same for every record, and all the records are checked in one request. The code-generated question keys contain each record's database ID:

Try it in the Playground →

The response:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.13.0",
  "answers": {
    "same_as_record_18": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.74
    },
    "same_as_record_42": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.09
    },
    "same_as_record_77": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.08
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 535,
    "output_tokens": 58
  }
}
```

Each answer is the probability that the resume is for the person in that record. Record 18 spells the name differently but matches on location and employer, and gets 0.74. Record 42 has the same name in a different city with a different employer, and gets 0.09. Record 77 is a similar name at the same location with a different employer, and gets 0.08. Threshold each value in your code, as in [Handling multiple Noul answers in code](#handling-multiple-noul-answers-in-code), and send the middle values to a person.

With the Python SDK, the questions are built from the candidate records. The question text is fixed and the record changes:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, TypeSafeClient

SAME_PERSON = "Is the resume for the same person as `potential_duplicate`?"


def duplicate_questions(candidates: list[dict]) -> dict[str, Noul]:
    """One Noul per candidate record, all asking the same question."""
    return {
        f"same_as_record_{candidate['id']}": Noul(
            instructions={
                "potential_duplicate": {
                    "name": candidate["name"],
                    "location": candidate["location"],
                    "last_employer": candidate["last_employer"],
                },
                "question": SAME_PERSON,
            },
        )
        for candidate in candidates
    }


def find_duplicates(resume: dict, candidates: list[dict]) -> list[str]:
    with TypeSafeClient() as client:
        response = client.system_one(
            model="jev-latest",
            state={"resume": resume},
            questions=duplicate_questions(candidates),
        )
    return [
        question_id
        for question_id, answer in response.answers.items()
        if answer.noul > 0.7
    ]
```

The [structured-data-extraction cascade cookbook](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md) uses structured instructions to verify an extracted record. Every field gets the same set of questions. Each question's `instructions` object has the question text in the `main_question` property. There are also `field_spec` and `extracted_field` properties that change for each field.

## Noul in the cookbooks

Take a look at our cookbooks to see apps using Noul questions:

* [Parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md) runs a 13-question regulatory checklist over one article in a single request.
* [Self-consistency: nouls](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/consistency_noul_cookbook.md) scores an insurance claim against a 15-question rubric and measures how stable the values are across runs.
* [Re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md) uses the probability itself, not a threshold: one Noul per query-candidate pair, then sorts candidates by the value.
* [Line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md) pairs a Choice that finds the matching line with a Noul that checks whether the document contains an answer at all.
* [Structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md) asks one Noul per pair of lines, whether a line break split a sentence, to rebuild paragraphs from plain text.
