Below is a request where the state is a support message and the two questions are whether the customer wants a person and whether they have contacted support before:

Try it in the Playground →

You choose the question ids, `is_human_escalation` and `is_repeat_contact` here. The ids are not sent to the model. Each answer is returned under the same id. The first question relies on `instructions` alone. The second adds `criteria` to say what counts as a yes and what counts as a no.

With the [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), the same questions are `Noul` objects:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, NoulCriteria, TypeSafeClient

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    response = client.system_one(
        model="jev-latest",
        state="I have asked three times now. Can I please just talk to a real person?",
        questions={
            "is_human_escalation": Noul(
                instructions="Is the customer asking for a human agent?",
            ),
            "is_repeat_contact": Noul(
                instructions="Has the customer contacted support about this before?",
                criteria=NoulCriteria(
                    true="Mentions a prior attempt, ticket, or that they have asked before",
                    false="No sign of any previous contact",
                ),
            ),
        },
    )

    print(response.answers["is_human_escalation"].noul)
    print(response.answers["is_repeat_contact"].noul)
```

The `system_one` method and the `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` endpoint are both named after [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), TypeSafe's AI model. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) covers where to use it in your code.

If you're using a coding agent, install the [TypeSafe agent skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill.md#installation) first so it knows the request and response shapes.

> [!NOTE]
>
> `instructions` can be a string, an object, or an array. Start with a string. Use an object when the question needs data alongside it, such as a record to compare the state against, or when part of the question is built by your code. [Use structure in the questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md#use-structure-in-the-questions) explains when structure helps, and [the example below](#structured-instructions) shows it with questions built in code.

## Response structure

The response has one entry in `answers` per question, under the ids from the request:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.13.0",
  "answers": {
    "is_human_escalation": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.99
    },
    "is_repeat_contact": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.93
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 360,
    "output_tokens": 39
  }
}
```

Both answers here are close to 1. The customer says "talk to a real person", so `is_human_escalation` is 0.99. "I have asked three times now" matches the `true` description of `is_repeat_contact`, so it is 0.93.

## Reading a Noul

The number is the answer and the certainty in one. A value near 1 is a strong yes. A value near 0 is a strong no. A value near 0.5 means the model gives yes and no similar probability.

The table below shows recorded `jev-1.13.0` answers to the `is_human_escalation` question for different customer messages:

| State | `noul` |
| - | - |
| Thanks, that fixed it! | 0.02 |
| How do I reset my password? | 0.07 |
| I need this sorted today, whatever it takes. | 0.26 |
| Are you a bot? | 0.40 |
| Is there any way to speak to someone about my invoice? | 0.84 |
| I have asked three times now. Can I please just talk to a real person? | 0.99 |

The first two and the last two are clear. "I need this sorted today" is urgent but never asks for a person, and gets 0.26. "Are you a bot?" hints at wanting a human without asking for one, and the model splits almost evenly at 0.40. Both are the kind of message where a decision needs to be made based on a threshold in your code.

There is no separate `confidence` value for a Noul, unlike a [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) or a [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md). A Noul's probability distribution has only two outcomes, yes and no, so the single `noul` value describes it completely. A Choice or Score spreads probability over several options or levels, and `confidence` summarizes that spread.

Most often your code thresholds `noul` into a boolean:

```python theme={null}
wants_human = response.answers["is_human_escalation"].noul > 0.9

if wants_human:
    route_to_agent(ticket)
else:
    route_to_bot(ticket)
```

A good starting point is 0.7 for yes and 0.3 for no. Often you only care whether the answer is yes, and 0.7 is the only threshold you need. Where to set it depends on the cost of being wrong. Raise it when acting on a false yes is expensive, such as paging someone or issuing a refund. Lower it when missing a true yes is expensive, such as failing to flag a safety issue. Avoid fitting thresholds closely to a handful of test cases. Values between 0.3 and 0.7 can go to a person rather than either code path. That is the same three-way split the [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md#three-paths-for-using-confidence-in-your-code) page describes for Choice and Score answers.

A Noul value runs from 0 to 1, but it's not a scale of the thing you asked about. It is the probability that the answer is yes. If the question is really about degree, the value does not measure the degree. Below, "Is the candidate strong in Python?" is asked about four candidates, next to a [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) with four levels: no experience, some familiarity, regular use in a job, deep expertise.

| Candidate | Noul: "Is the candidate strong in Python?" | Score: "How much Python experience does the candidate have?" |
| - | - | - |
| My experience is in Java and Go. I have not used Python. | 0.03 | 0.0 (No experience) |
| I have used Python occasionally for small scripts alongside my main Java work. | 0.14 | 1.0 (Some familiarity) |
| I used Python every day for two years in my last job, mostly data pipelines. | 0.81 | 2.05 (Regular use in a job) |
| I have written Python daily for eight years, including maintaining a large Django codebase. | 0.92 | 2.89 (Deep expertise) |

The Noul judges one proposition, "strong", and the values are how likely it is. You could create levels in the 0 to 1 range in your code, such as 0.3 to 0.7 for "some experience", but the model will not see them, so nothing in the answer was judged against them. A middle value can mean medium experience or an unclear case, and the spacing between candidates is not something you chose. The Score judges each level description on its own, so every candidate landed on or near a level you wrote, and the returned probabilities show how the model divided its judgment between levels. If you disagree, reword a level and run it again. [Choose a question type](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives#choose-a-question-type) explains the distinction.

## Writing a Noul question

Ask one yes/no question per Noul. If a question has two conditions, such as "Is the customer angry and asking for a refund?", the model has to judge both at once and the value means less. Ask two Nouls and combine them in code.

Phrase the question so that a high value means yes. "Does the message contain personal data?" is clear. "Is the message free of personal data?" inverts the meaning, and code that reads it later will get it backwards.

A statement works as well as a question. For "The customer is requesting a refund", a value near 1 means the statement is true. Try both phrasings with your own data to see which works better.

Make the boundary between yes and no unambiguous. "Does this candidate have any Python experience?" works well because "any" leaves no middle ground. When the boundary is subtle, add `criteria` with `true` and `false` descriptions, as the `is_repeat_contact` question above does. The instruction is enough for most Nouls, so try your questions with and without `criteria` and keep whichever gives better answers on your documents.

## Good practice: ask more than one question per call

For a checklist of conditions, ask many Noul questions in one request: one question per condition, and the code decides what the combination means. Questions are evaluated in parallel, so adding Nouls barely changes the response time. [Ask multiple questions together](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives#ask-***) explains this in more detail.

## Handling multiple Noul answers in code

The two-question request above gives the code enough to route the message. The example below escalates to a person when the customer asks for one, and raises the priority when they have been in touch before. A value in the middle on either question goes to a reviewer instead of a code path:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, NoulCriteria, TypeSafeClient

SUPPORT_QUESTIONS = {
    "is_human_escalation": Noul(
        instructions="Is the customer asking for a human agent?",
    ),
    "is_repeat_contact": Noul(
        instructions="Has the customer contacted support about this before?",
        criteria=NoulCriteria(
            true="Mentions a prior attempt, ticket, or that they have asked before",
            false="No sign of any previous contact",
        ),
    ),
}

YES = 0.7
NO = 0.3


def route(message: str) -> None:
    with TypeSafeClient() as client:
        response = client.system_one(
            model="jev-latest",
            state=message,
            questions=SUPPORT_QUESTIONS,
        )
    answers = response.answers

    wants_human = answers["is_human_escalation"].noul
    repeat = answers["is_repeat_contact"].noul

    if NO < wants_human < YES or NO < repeat < YES:
        # The model isn't sure either way. Let a person decide.
        send_to_review(message)
        return

    priority = "high" if repeat >= YES else "normal"
    if wants_human >= YES:
        route_to_agent(message, priority=priority)
    else:
        route_to_bot(message, priority=priority)
```

For the message above, the noul answer value for `is_human_escalation` is 0.99 and `is_repeat_contact` is 0.93, so the code routes it to an agent at high priority. The message "How do I reset my password?" is 0.07 on both questions and is routed to the bot.

The thresholds live in your code. If reviewers see too many messages, narrow the gap between `NO` and `YES`. If too many wrong routes get through, widen it. If you later need to know whether the message mentions a payment, or whether it contains personal data, add another Noul to `SUPPORT_QUESTIONS`. The request count stays at one.

## Structured instructions

Instructions can be an object instead of a string, with the question in one field and supplementary data in the others. [Use structure in the questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md#use-structure-in-the-questions) covers when that helps. Here it's used for a question built using code: a resume that has just arrived is compared against records in a candidate database that might be the same person. Each record goes into a `potential_duplicate` field as it is, the `question` is the same for every record, and all the records are checked in one request. The code-generated question keys contain each record's database ID:

Try it in the Playground →

The response:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.13.0",
  "answers": {
    "same_as_record_18": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.74
    },
    "same_as_record_42": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.09
    },
    "same_as_record_77": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.08
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 535,
    "output_tokens": 58
  }
}
```

Each answer is the probability that the resume is for the person in that record. Record 18 spells the name differently but matches on location and employer, and gets 0.74. Record 42 has the same name in a different city with a different employer, and gets 0.09. Record 77 is a similar name at the same location with a different employer, and gets 0.08. Threshold each value in your code, as in [Handling multiple Noul answers in code](#handling-multiple-noul-answers-in-code), and send the middle values to a person.

With the Python SDK, the questions are built from the candidate records. The question text is fixed and the record changes:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, TypeSafeClient

SAME_PERSON = "Is the resume for the same person as `potential_duplicate`?"


def duplicate_questions(candidates: list[dict]) -> dict[str, Noul]:
    """One Noul per candidate record, all asking the same question."""
    return {
        f"same_as_record_{candidate['id']}": Noul(
            instructions={
                "potential_duplicate": {
                    "name": candidate["name"],
                    "location": candidate["location"],
                    "last_employer": candidate["last_employer"],
                },
                "question": SAME_PERSON,
            },
        )
        for candidate in candidates
    }


def find_duplicates(resume: dict, candidates: list[dict]) -> list[str]:
    with TypeSafeClient() as client:
        response = client.system_one(
            model="jev-latest",
            state={"resume": resume},
            questions=duplicate_questions(candidates),
        )
    return [
        question_id
        for question_id, answer in response.answers.items()
        if answer.noul > 0.7
    ]
```

The [structured-data-extraction cascade cookbook](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md) uses structured instructions to verify an extracted record. Every field gets the same set of questions. Each question's `instructions` object has the question text in the `main_question` property. There are also `field_spec` and `extracted_field` properties that change for each field.

## Noul in the cookbooks

Take a look at our cookbooks to see apps using Noul questions:

* [Parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md) runs a 13-question regulatory checklist over one article in a single request.
* [Self-consistency: nouls](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/consistency_noul_cookbook.md) scores an insurance claim against a 15-question rubric and measures how stable the values are across runs.
* [Re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md) uses the probability itself, not a threshold: one Noul per query-candidate pair, then sorts candidates by the value.
* [Line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md) pairs a Choice that finds the matching line with a Noul that checks whether the document contains an answer at all.
* [Structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md) asks one Noul per pair of lines, whether a line break split a sentence, to rebuild paragraphs from plain text.

===== cron =====
Configure and manage scheduled tasks.

Schedule recurring, one-shot, or interval-based tasks using cron expressions, RFC 3339 timestamps, durations, or fixed intervals.

Cron expressions use the standard 5-field format: 'min hour day month weekday'. Timezones default to UTC; override with --tz and an IANA timezone name.

This is a massive rename. The user wants "zeroclaw" removed from everything except the binary. No other files should be touched.

The user's latest message overrides the adapter naming in AGENTS.md. zeroclow_router and tched_router should become threetched. The binary itself remains zeroclaw.

The user's absolute "no tched" rule risks collapsing the 3tched versus threetched distinction. The rename likely applies only to the zeroclow_* and tched_router bridge names.

The 3tched filesystem will stay as-is. I will wait for the current cargo check to finish before renaming bridge adapters. I will explain the exact scope of changes first.

A naive replace of "tched" is dangerous because "threetched" contains that substring. I will count distinct identifiers to scope the rename precisely. Editing files during the current cargo check is safe; the build will simply fail on a mixed state.

I will kill the in-flight cargo check to release the lock. The rename will target only zeroclow* and zeroclaw* identifiers in our code, leaving upstream binary strings untouched.

tched_router will become threetched across plugin IDs, modules, proto definitions, and types. The existing threetched plugin is the passthrough schema; merging tched_router into it is intentional. This is a large architectural rename rather than a simple string replacement.

The hand-rolled tched_router.rs is large and still actively used by zeroclow_router_runtime.rs.

The user is clarifying terminology.

Socat was the old pattern for no-NIC containers, bridging a host socket to an internal TCP port. The current bridge binds its own listeners directly: a TLS door on 10.0.0.2:8090, a gRPC socket at /run/opdbus/grpc.sock, a shared container socket, and an EMQX exhook on 127.0.0.1:9000.

Socat is the traditional tool for that. It relays one socket to another: a TCP port to a Unix socket, or one port to a different address. It does not translate gRPC. Tonic still does that.

The bridge no longer uses socat for its own listeners. It binds `10.0.0.2:8090`, `/run/opdbus/grpc.sock`, and `127.0.0.1:9000` itself. Socat remains the old pattern for a container with no NIC, where a port inside the container is relayed through a shared Unix socket.
not called dmux

The user clarified that port-splitting is not called "dmux" (demux).

The user wants the correct term for socat's port-splitting function. It is a multipurpose relay or socket relay.

The operation is a relay or port forward. It is not a demux. The ghostbridge mux demultiplexes by peer credential.

The word is **relay**. Socat’s own description is “multipurpose relay”: it accepts a connection on one address and connects it to another.

A demux is a different job. It looks at one stream and separates the protocols inside it. The port split does not do that.

A MUX (short for multiplexer) is a hardware device or circuit that combines multiple analog or digital input signals into a single, shared output line or transmission medium.

How It Works

• Many-to-One: It takes several separate data streams and merges them so they can travel across a single cable, fiber optic strand, or wireless frequency.
• Control / Select Lines: It uses specific control signals to determine which input passes through to the output at any given moment.
• DEMUX Pairing: At the receiving end, a DEMUX (demultiplexer) performs the reverse process by splitting the single combined signal back into its original individual streams.

The user provided a definition of MUX and DEMUX.

The user is mapping the MUX/DEMUX distinction to their socat relay system.

The bridge binds multiple listeners to a single port. This is the MUX side of the architecture.

The bridge binds several separate addresses. This is not a true MUX or DEMUX. Each listener is an independent socket. The ghostbridge mux was demultiplexed by SO_PEERCRED. That was called a mux in the codebase but does not match the user's definition.

The user suggests the ai_ prefix might be a Cargo.toml alias rather than a file rename.

Cargo.toml cannot alias internal module paths. Package renames, library names, and target names only affect dependencies or external targets. Rust has no feature that maps one module path to another.

The `#[path]` attribute is the Rust equivalent. It lets a module keep its existing filename while resolving under a different name. This still requires a `mod` declaration in lib.rs.

No. A `Cargo.toml` alias cannot rename a module inside the bridge.

Cargo can rename a dependency crate, a `[[bin]]` target, or a `[[test]]` target. `op-grpc-bridge` already does that for tests, including `tched_router_integration`. Those names do not change `crate::zeroclow_own_agent_route` or the other route modules.

A second name without moving the file is a Rust alias in `lib.rs`:

```rust
#[path = "zeroclow_own_agent_route.rs"]
mod ai_agent_route;
```

That makes `ai_agent_route` the module name and leaves the file where it is. The old `mod zeroclow_own_agent_route` line has to go, or both names stay visible.

name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  TypeSafe integration craft for System One models (sometimes called Decision Models) such as Jev,
  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.
---

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→
## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests
170→
**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
180→question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers
190→
### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

200→- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
210→  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
220→  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong
230→
Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
240→jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:
250→
- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks
260→
Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
270→  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
280→  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".

  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our

  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.

  time", rather than as "not late".

  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.

If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.

## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests

**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers

### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong

Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:

- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks

Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

1→# Golden deploy and live cutover (2026-09-20)
User reversed an earlier “use existing `target/release` only” plan: **build, then deploy**.

User reversed an earlier “use existing `target/release` only” plan: **build, then deploy**. Golden prep is artifacts only — no live-copy onto running processes, no network-service restarts. Post-build sequence: reseal catalog → persist catalog → populate golden. Parallel artifacts: workspace release build, native router, UI.

Live activation (user later required all deployed, not staging only): read-only golden snapshot → `btrfs send/receive` → install **only MANIFEST binaries** (skip leftover retired binaries) → restart **application** services. Do not touch OVS, uplink, DHCP, session bus, emqx, mongodb-mcp-server, or mail-3tched (`apply-rootfs` is offline-image only). Keep the **live** `op-grpc-bridge` run script; the golden copy requires a runtime token that is missing on this host. Swapping the script without that token is unsafe. New catalog and new bridge binary are coupled.

- Post-build catalog: `opblob seal-shm` + `persist`; **66 plugins**; generation **45092**; SHM/disk hash `b0b418c9…6c35`; retired plugin id `factory` swept.
- Golden restage: `/opt/op-dbus/golden` (28 binaries, catalog, native, UI, EMQX, nlm, MongoDB MCP, runit defs). MANIFEST commit `a14c9cf`, build `20260920T011233Z`.
10→- Golden snapshot: `/opt/op-dbus/golden-ro-20260920T011233Z`. Rollback: `/var/tmp/op-dbus-predeploy-20260920T011757Z`.
- This host does not treat golden prep as install: live `/usr/local/bin/op-grpc-bridge` stayed the Sep 9 binary until the later cutover.
- Live after cutover: `op-grpc-bridge` on both `127.0.0.1:8090` and `10.0.0.3:8090` (ready file present), `op-web` `:8080`, `opdbus-grants`, `op-of-controller`, `tched-router` (`zeroclaw`), `op-runit-systemctl`. Catalog generation 45092, 66 plugins.
- Runtime paths for the new socket checks: `/run/opdbus/grpc.sock`, `/run/ghostbridge` (must be `0755`, not `1777`), `/run/ghostbridge/.projection.lock`.

## Bridge crash-loop and source fixes

First look was a projection lock. Actual fatal path: new `op-grpc-bridge` died parking identity CTs `bea37ecb…` / `f036f8d8…` that Incus already had in **ERROR** / already stopped. Parking used to fail closed.

Fixes (left uncommitted in running binary `4d7546fed80c53d7`, then committed and pushed as **`5bcd809`**): treat already-stopped / Error as parked; **build the axum app once and clone it** for the dual TCP binds so the MCP policy owner is not installed twice. Rebuild and redeploy the fixed binary — golden swap alone is not enough. Stale `/run/opdbus/grpc.sock` and `/run/ghostbridge` mode `1777` failed new socket checks: remove the socket, set dir `0755`, create `.projection.lock`.
20→
Also pushed **`5912a5f`** (Incus pool recovery note). Crate graphs stayed uncommitted.

1→# odbus-verified TypeSafe Jev
How odbus-verified calls Jev, and Salad versus Grok or OpenRouter for bulk sweeps.

## Skill and call path

- In odbus-verified, the Jev skill is `.agents/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md`; there is no separate jev skill.
- Jev is called through native typed `judge`/`judge_batch` after reading `xd://eval/judge`, using model role `typesafe/jev-latest` and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.
- It judges evidence only and must not route models or authorize mutations.
- The routing-specific jev-router skill is intentionally not loaded.
10→
## Live API

- Live HTTP API is POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with Bearer auth.
- Question types are noul, choice, score, and box.
- Project audits record models such as typesafe/jev-1.14.0 and typesafe/jev-1.13.0.
- Ask permission before live test calls.
- Do not treat confidence as the sole action gate.
- Rename-scan calls use TYPESAFE_API_KEY from ~/.bash_secrets (never print it), POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest.
- For that scan, act on noul only if >= 0.7, reject if <= 0.3, else abstain.
20→- Use a cheap high-volume model for the JEV swarm so a run does not die on a rate limit mid-swarm.
- This Grok session can launch only grok-4.7, grok-4.7-build-fast, grok-4.6, and grok-4.5. GPT-6 Luna is not callable here even though it is the cheap high-volume option (~$0.10/M input, $0.50/M output). fork_secondary_model in ~/.grok/config.toml is grok-4.6.
- The line-by-line name pass uses jev-latest on the TypeSafe API, a rate limit separate from Grok.
- For bulk swarm or line-by-line work, do not spend the Grok quota.

name: grpc-expert
description: "Expert guidance for gRPC/Protocol Buffers work in the operation-dbus-proto (OP-DBUS) workspace — designing plugin methods, generating .proto/service definitions, wiring the op-grpc-bridge, or fixing plugins with missing gRPC methods. Use this whenever the user mentions gRPC, proto/protobuf, plugin methods, the gRPC bridge, tonic, reflection descriptors, 'missing plugins' in the gRPC diagnostic page, or the seal/freeze/hot pipeline — even if they don't say 'gRPC' explicitly (e.g. 'the plugin isn't showing up on the diagnostic page', 'add a method to plugin X', 'regen protos')."
metadata:
  version: 1.0.0
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# gRPC Expert — OP-DBUS
10→
This workspace does **not** hand-write per-plugin `.proto` files. Proto generation is
automatic, driven entirely by each plugin's `PluginSchema`. If you remember one thing
from this skill: **fixing a plugin's gRPC surface means editing its Rust schema
function, not writing `.proto`.**

## The real pipeline (roll → seal → freeze → hot)

```
1. Plugin declares  → PluginSchema { methods: HashMap<String, MethodDecl>, signals: Vec<SignalDecl>, ... }
20→                       in crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<plugin>.rs
2. Schema gets put   → op-projection's SchemaEngine publishes the catalog hash
                       (op_identity::schema_bridge::schema_catalog_hash())
3. Sealed by blob    → op-blob seals the plugin object into an immutable blob:
                       /dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob
                       (op-blob is the ONLY writer — never write blobs elsewhere)
```

root = Path("/srv/git/odbus-verified/crates/op-grpc-bridge")
replacements = [
    ("zeroclow_router_admission_tests", "chat_router_admission_tests"),
    ("zeroclow_router_generation_native", "chat_router_generation"),
    ("zeroclow_router_legacy_dispatch", "chat_router_legacy_dispatch"),
    ("zeroclow_router_object_blob", "chat_router_object_blob"),
    ("zeroclow_router_admission", "chat_router_admission"),
    ("zeroclow_router_runtime", "chat_router_runtime"),
    ("zeroclow_catalog_binding", "chat_router_catalog_binding"),
    ("zeroclow_config_dispatch", "chat_router_config_dispatch"),
    ("zeroclow_config_engine", "chat_router_config_engine"),
    ("zeroclow_config_secret_policy", "chat_router_config_secret_policy"),
    ("zeroclow_own_agent_route", "chat_router_agent_route"),

    ("zeroclow_router", "chat_router"),

    ("tched_router_contract", "chat_router_contract"),
]

changed = []
for path in root.rglob("*"):
    if path.suffix not in {".rs", ".proto", ".toml"} or not path.is_file():

    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    updated = text
    for old, new in replacements:

        path.write_text(updated, encoding="utf-8")
        changed.append(str(path.relative_to(root)))

print(f"updated {len(changed)} files")
for name in changed:
    print(name)

content.text:
The user is asking whether the chat router pulls in old names.

The chat router is only partially responsible. It stamps old router spellings like `3tched-router` and `tched-router` into the plugin schema as sealed identifiers. It also reads environment variables such as `TCHED_ROUTER_ENDPOINT` and `TCHED_ROUTER_CONFIG_DIR`.

The bridge runtime and server still read old environment variables like `ZEROCLOW_ROUTER_RUNTIME_*` and `ZEROCLOW_ROUTER_BIND_ADDR`. These are the router's runtime door, not imported by the plugin file. Comments in `chat_router_contract.rs` and `chat_router_legacy_methods.rs` also reference prior names. Container names such as `zeroclowChatbot`, `zeroclowCtlChatbot`, pool `zeroclow-pool`, and profile `zeroclow-lungs` are not pulled by the chat router.

The chat router is what still pulls the old router names in. It is not what pulls in the container, filesystem, or site names.

The plugin file `chat_router.rs` does not say `zeroclow` or `ZeroClaw`. What it does stamp into the schema is `3tched-router` on most capabilities, and `tched-router` on a smaller set: selection, catalog binding, agent route, and router read/write. It also reads `TCHED_ROUTER_ENDPOINT`, `TCHED_ROUTER_GRPC_TARGET`, and `TCHED_ROUTER_CONFIG_DIR`.

The bridge process that hosts that router still reads the older environment names: `ZEROCLOW_ROUTER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT`, `ZEROCLOW_ROUTER_BIND_ADDR`, `ZEROCLOW_ROUTER_UNIX_SOCKET`, `ZEROCLOW_ROUTER_PLUGIN_ID`, and the TLS variables next to them. Those are live lookups, not the comments added so a search can find the old file names.

These are separate and do not come from the chat router: `zeroclowChatbot`, `zeroclow-pool`, `zeroclow-lungs`, `zeroclowfs`, `zeroclow.com`, and `vendor/zeroclow-json-render-ui`.

import os, json, time
roots=[
"/home/jeremy/.omp/agent/sessions/--srv-git-odbus-verified--",
"/home/jeremy/.grok/sessions",
"/tmp",
]
# search only recent files for exact workspace cargo outcomes
keys=("cargo check --workspace","cargo build --workspace","cargo build --release --workspace")
cutoff=time.mktime(time.strptime("2026-10-26 04:00","%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"))
found=0
for root in roots:
    if not os.path.isdir(root):
        continue
    for dirpath, dirs, files in os.walk(root):
        # prune huge trees
        base=os.path.basename(dirpath)
        if base in {".git","target","node_modules","deps"}:
            dirs.clear()
            continue
        for name in files:
            if not name.endswith(('.jsonl','.log','.txt')):
                continue
            path=os.path.join(dirpath,name)
            try:
                st=os.stat(path)
            except OSError:
                continue
            if st.st_mtime < cutoff or st.st_size > 80_000_000:
                continue
            try:
                with open(path, errors='replace') as f:
                    blob=f.read()
            except OSError:
                continue
            if "cargo check --workspace" not in blob and "cargo build --workspace" not in blob:
                continue
            # extract nearby finished/killed
            idx=0
            while True:
                i=blob.find("cargo check --workspace", idx)
                j=blob.find("cargo build --workspace", idx)
                cands=[x for x in (i,j) if x>=0]
                if not cands:
                    break
                k=min(cands)
                snippet=blob[k:k+500].replace('\n',' | ')
                print(f"\n== {path} @{k}")
                print(snippet[:450])
                found+=1
                idx=k+20
                if found>40:
                    raise SystemExit
print("\nTOTAL", found)
PY

import os, time, tomllib
from pathlib import Path
root=Path("/srv/git/odbus-verified")
ws=tomllib.loads((root/"Cargo.toml").read_text())
members=ws["workspace"]["members"]
# exclude virtual patterns if any
pkgs=[]
for m in members:
    man=root/m/"Cargo.toml"
    if not man.exists():
        print("MISSING", m)
        continue
    data=tomllib.loads(man.read_text())
    name=data["package"]["name"]
    lib=name.replace("-","_")
    newest=0
    newest_path=""
    for dirpath, dirs, files in os.walk(root/m):
        dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if d not in {"target",".git"}]
        for fn in files:
            if fn.endswith((".rs",".proto",".toml")) or fn=="build.rs":
                p=os.path.join(dirpath, fn)
                try:
                    mt=os.stat(p).st_mtime
                except OSError:
                    continue
                if mt>newest:
                    newest=mt
                    newest_path=p
    def newest_art(base, prefixes):
        best=0
        bestp=""
        dep=Path(base)
        if not dep.is_dir():
            return 0,""
        for pref in prefixes:
            for p in dep.glob(pref+"-*"):
                if p.suffix not in {".rlib",".rmeta",".d"} and not p.name.endswith(".rmeta"):
                    # binaries have no suffix sometimes
                    pass
                try:
                    mt=p.stat().st_mtime
                    sz=p.stat().st_size
                except OSError:
                    continue
                if sz==0:
                    continue
                if mt>best:
                    best=mt
                    bestp=str(p)
        return best, bestp
    targets=[
        ("debug", root/"target/debug/deps", (f"lib{lib}",)),
        ("gnu-debug", root/"target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/deps", (f"lib{lib}",)),
        ("release", root/"target/release/deps", (f"lib{lib}",)),
        ("gnu-release", root/"target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/deps", (f"lib{lib}",)),
    ]
    rows=[]
    for label, base, prefs in targets:
        mt,p=newest_art(base, prefs)
        rows.append((label, mt))
    # also bins: look at package targets
    bins=[]
    for t in data.get("bin", []) if isinstance(data.get("bin"), list) else []:
        bins.append(t.get("name"))
    if "[[bin]]" in man.read_text() or data.get("bin"):
        pass
    def fmt(mt):
        if not mt:
            return "none"
        return time.strftime("%m-%d %H:%M", time.gmtime(mt))
    src=fmt(newest)
    stale=[]
    for label, mt in rows:
        if mt and mt+1 >= newest:
            stale.append(f"{label}:{fmt(mt)} OK")
        elif mt:
            stale.append(f"{label}:{fmt(mt)} OLD")
        else:
            stale.append(f"{label}:none")
    print(f"{name:28} src {src}  " + "  ".join(stale))
print("---root package---")
print("members", len(members))
